articles.title: What a PDF xref table actually is, read through qpdf --show-xref before and after object streams
articles.excerpt: Run qpdf --show-xref on a plain text-only PDF and every line looks like 2/0: uncompressed; offset = 131. Rewrite the file with --object-streams=generate, run it again, and the second line reads 2/0: c…
articles.body: Run qpdf --show-xref on a plain text-only PDF and every line looks like 2/0: uncompressed; offset = 131 . Rewrite the file with --object-streams=generate , run it again, and the second line reads 2/0: compressed; stream = 1, index = 0 . In this test the file went from 137,782 to 132,065 bytes, 4.15% smaller, same 10 pages, same text. I knew the words "xref table" and "object stream" but couldn't have explained that one-line change, so here is the beginner's model that made it readable, plus the part I didn't expect: 4% is close to the ceiling for this file. The test file is a 10-page text-only report with fictional content and an embedded Chinese font subset, run once on one Apple-silicon Mac with qpdf 12.4.0, so every number means "this file, this run".
articles.author: yue xing

articles.title: Our portal releases went out without the new index.html whenever it kept the same size
articles.excerpt: Our depot portal is a single page app served from an S3 bucket. A build job produces the static files, and a deploy job puts them in the bucket with aws s3 sync. The JavaScript bundles have a content…
articles.body: Our depot portal is a single page app served from an S3 bucket. A build job produces the static files, and a deploy job puts them in the bucket with aws s3 sync. The JavaScript bundles have a content hash in their file names, so a new build gets new bundle files and a new index.html that points at them. Old bundles stay in the bucket for a few releases, so pages already open keep working. In September we made our build artifacts reproducible. The build job now packs the output with GNU tar using --sort=name, fixed owners and --mtime set to the first of January 1980, so the same commit always gives a tarball with the same checksum. The deploy job extracts it, and tar restores the stored modification times, as it does by default.

articles.title: Why I Built an Ad-Free, 4K Video Downloader in Next.js 14 & Python (And Killed Popups Forever)
articles.excerpt: Have you ever tried downloading a public video from Reddit or an educational lecture from YouTube recently? You type "video downloader" into Google, click on one of the top results, and within 3 secon…
articles.body: Have you ever tried downloading a public video from Reddit or an educational lecture from YouTube recently? You type "video downloader" into Google, click on one of the top results, and within 3 seconds: Three sketchy popups open in background tabs. You see 4 blinking green "DOWNLOAD NOW" buttons (3 of which are adware installers). You finally download the Reddit video, only to discover it has no sound because Reddit serves video and audio on separate streams. As a full-stack engineer, I got sick of this hostile user experience. The web shouldn't feel like navigating a minefield just to grab an offline copy of a creative commons video, a transcript, or a TikTok tutorial without a giant watermark plastered over it.

articles.title: Shipping an LLM feature to production: a 6-step checklist from real client projects
articles.excerpt: Most LLM prototypes look great in a demo and fall apart the first week real users touch them. Over the last two years our team has taken a number of these prototypes into production for clients in log…
articles.body: Most LLM prototypes look great in a demo and fall apart the first week real users touch them. Over the last two years our team has taken a number of these prototypes into production for clients in logistics, healthcare and retail. The failures were rarely about the model. They were about everything around it. Here is the checklist we now run before any LLM feature ships. 1. Define what "correct" means before writing a prompt Write 30-50 real example inputs with the answer a domain expert would accept. This becomes your evaluation set. Without it, every prompt change is a guess. 2. Put retrieval quality ahead of model choice For most business use cases, the answer is already in the company's documents.

articles.title: More of the AI in Your Product May Run on the User's Own Device
articles.excerpt: For the past few years, adding AI to a product has usually meant sending the user's text or images to a large model in a data centre and waiting for the answer. That is starting to change. More and mo…
articles.body: For the past few years, adding AI to a product has usually meant sending the user's text or images to a large model in a data centre and waiting for the answer. That is starting to change. More and more of it can now run on the phone or laptop in front of the user. The hardware is arriving quietly. Many new phones and laptops include a chip designed for machine learning, often called a neural processing unit. Microsoft's Copilot+ PCs, introduced in 2024, require one capable of at least forty trillion operations per second. Apple's own AI features use a model of around three billion parameters that runs on the device, sending only harder requests to its servers.

articles.title: Bar, blots and the larger-die rule: how I coded backgammon in JavaScript
articles.excerpt: A player once told me my backgammon was broken because it wouldn't let them play their 2. They were right that it wouldn't. They were wrong that it was broken. With that roll, the only way to use both…
articles.body: A player once told me my backgammon was broken because it wouldn't let them play their 2. They were right that it wouldn't. They were wrong that it was broken. With that roll, the only way to use both dice was 6 first, and the rules say you have to use both dice if you can. That rule, and a few like it, made backgammon take longer than games that look far harder. Here's how I coded the rules for the backgammon on mympgames , my free multiplayer browser arcade. Everything lives in one plain file, backgammon-rules.js . The server uses it to judge legality, and the browser loads the same file in a Web Worker for the bot. Excerpts are real code, lightly trimmed.

articles.title: How we made 78 jewelry products indexable by moving off hash routing to Next.js
articles.excerpt: A client came to us with a beautiful fine-jewelry storefront that had one fatal none of its products could The site was an older single-page app that used hash routing. Every product /jewelry#product/…
articles.body: A client came to us with a beautiful fine-jewelry storefront that had one fatal flaw for a business that lives on organic search: none of its products could rank on Google. The site was an older single-page app that used hash routing. Every product lived at a URL like: /jewelry#product/210-104 It looked fine to a human. To a search engine, it was a problem. Why hash URLs kill SEO Everything after the # in a URL is a fragment — it's handled entirely in the browser and is never sent to the server . Googlebot sees one page ( /jewelry ) and all 78 products collapse into it. There are no distinct, crawlable URLs to index, no per-product titles, no per-product metadata. So the catalogue was effectively invisible.

articles.title: 53 Years Later, The Greatest Closing Line In Sci-Fi History Is Still The Best Book Quote Of The 1970s
articles.excerpt: Roadside Picnic ends with one of science fiction’s most beautiful lines, a simple wish for happiness that still resonates more than 50 years later.
articles.body: The canon of science-fiction literature is home to countless unforgettable endings, from 1984 ’s short but devastating retrospective ("He loved Big Brother") to The Three-Body Problem ’s defiant reminder that humanity cannot be so easily wiped out. The best sci-fi endings don't offer comfortable closure. Instead, they reframe everything that came before. In their closing lines, great sci-fi novelists leave readers suspended in the aftermath, forced to stew in the terrifying logic of cold technology, the fragility of human nature, and the vast expanse of space.

articles.body: PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth , something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary. Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2 , flew past Neptune. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

articles.title: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
articles.excerpt: A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a tower's-eye view of the first-ever catch of a Starship upper stage, a milestone SpaceX achieved last weekend.
articles.body: A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage. The company notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms. You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower. The Ship upper stage of SpaceX's Starship megarocket comes back to its launch tower for a "chopsticks" catch on Nov. 14, 2026, during the vehicle's 15th test flight.
